query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled post‐casting annealing treatment that induces an in situ, fine, ductile intergranular phase will improve the mechanical integrity of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 without sacrificing its large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 in the as-cast condition exhibits high caloric performance but poor structural integrity with a tendency to crack.
generation.intervention: Apply a targeted heat treatment (annealing at around 500°C for an optimized short duration under inert atmosphere) to promote the precipitation of a fine, ductile phase along grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: The intervention is valid under conditions of applied magnetic and pressure fields and within the temperature and loading regimes used to evaluate the caloric effect. Tests should include room temperature compressive loading and operational temperatures relevant to the caloric response.
generation.structural_mediator: Intrinsically formed, fine-scale ductile intergranular precipitates that reinforce grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The ductile phase is expected to act as a crack deflector and energy absorber during deformation, enhancing toughness and compressive strength. Since the treatment is modest in temperature and duration, it minimally alters the crystallographic and energetic landscape responsible for the large caloric response.
generation.predicted_outcome: An improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., compressive strength increased by roughly 1.5–2× compared to the as-cast state) while retaining a caloric effect magnitude comparable to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: The untreated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits a high caloric response but suffers from poor integrity and cracking under mechanical stress.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective only when the annealing parameters are carefully optimized to avoid phase transitions or coarsening that could degrade the caloric response. It must be applied under the same operational fields (magnetic/pressure) and temperature ranges used to measure the caloric performance.
generation.uncertainty: The exact annealing temperature, time, and the volume fraction/distribution of the ductile phase needed to maximize mechanical improvements without impacting the caloric effect still require optimization. The balance between strengthening and retention of caloric responsiveness is uncertain until these processing parameters are finely tuned.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 samples: one set remains as-cast (control) and the other set undergoes the prescribed annealing treatment. Under identical conditions of applied magnetic and pressure fields and relevant temperature ranges, measure mechanical properties (such as compressive strength and fracture toughness) and the caloric response (e.g., caloric effect amplitude and transition temperatures). Use microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM) to confirm the presence and distribution of the ductile intergranular phase.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (to assess ductile phase formation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., compressive strength increased by at least 1.5×) relative to the as-cast samples, or if the caloric response is degraded by more than approximately 10%, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Most rare earth oxides can be obtained in more than one structure type (polymorph) at ambient conditions: normally an A-type La2O3 and Nd2O3 can be synthesized in a C-type structure [] at temperatures below ~500 °C (and C-type was predicted [] to be their ground state structure); while normally C-type oxides from Dy to Yb were obtained in B-type structure in nanoparticles []. The oxides of trivalent actinides also found in these structure types []. Two high temperature structures were first identified by Foex and Traverse [,]. The H-type is hexagonal (P63/mmc) [] and was reported for all rare earth and Y sesquioxides except Lu and Yb []. For oxides from La to Dy, the transformation of the hexagonal phase to the cubic X-type (Im-3m) structure was detected before melting []. The X-type structure was also reported to be formed in Tm2O3 and Lu2O3 after irradiation with Xe and Au ion beams [].
